title: Unsupervised Multimodal Reward Modeling

paper.title: Unsupervised Multimodal Reward Modeling
paper.abstract: Abstract Vision-language reward models are trained on annotated preference pairs, which are expensive to collect and can disagree with each other, and are ranked by benchmark accuracy. We build one with no human preference label: a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone, trained to score a web caption above a perturbed version of the same caption; labeled data enters only to select the layer. The layer is the decisive choice, worth 5.8 points over the last layer, and one recipe transferred without re-tuning beats or at least matches GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B, 6.6 points ahead on VL-RewardBench, from a few thousand parameters at about a thousandth of fine-tuning compute. At an equal pair budget, perturbations teach a frozen head 3 to 5 points more than curated RLAIF-V pairs. Because the backbone is frozen the objective is convex and the perturbation sampler specifies the reward, which the benchmark does not identify: two heads trained on disjoint halves of the same perturbations tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. Retraining the head on the policy’s own verifier-labelled candidates cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points and lifts image-generation pass rate by 5.4, while scoring lower on every reward benchmark. Together, an intermediate-layer probe, free same-image perturbations and a verifier-driven bootstrap turn give a recipe for multimodal reward modeling that needs no annotator, costs a fraction of fine-tuning, and is specified by the comparisons it is trained on rather than by a benchmark rank.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning from human feedback ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) has made the reward model the channel through which preferences enter post-training. For vision-language models the same design is now standard: a scalar scorer over an image, a prompt and a response, trained on annotated preference pairs and ranked on preference benchmarks ( Yasunaga et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ) . The design has two costs: multimodal preference pairs are expensive to annotate and the annotations disagree with each other ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Once the model is built, benchmark accuracy is how it is compared, selected and trusted. VL-RewardBench accuracy correlates with Best-of- N N accuracy on MMMU-Pro for generative judges (Pearson’s r > 0.9 r>0.9 ; Li et al., 2025 ); what sets that number for a scalar reward model, and when it stops predicting deployment, is the question this paper takes up. Text reward models show that a reward is a comparison before it is a number: Bradley–Terry training identifies a reward only up to a shift that may differ across prompts ( Bradley and Terry, 1952 ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , so a score of .8 has no stable meaning across prompts, candidate pools or checkpoints. The scalar hides the relative preference that was always the operative signal ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Zhang, 2026 ) , so what a reward model learns is set by which comparisons it is trained on. And those comparisons need no annotator: web continuations as chosen against in-batch continuations as rejected train a text reward model with no label at all ( Fan et al., 2026 ) . We take both findings to the vision-language setting, make the comparison the object of study, and remove the human labels entirely. The reward model is a linear head on the hidden states of an intermediate layer of a frozen backbone, trained by in-batch Bradley–Terry ( Bradley and Terry, 1952 ) against same-image perturbations of web captions or same-seed re-renders of a perturbed prompt ( Fig. 2 , Section 2 ). The claim is about the training data: the probe layer is selected on one labeled benchmark, which we therefore treat as development and never as transfer evidence, and the loop of Section 3.4 uses verifier labels, not annotators. Two things then decide what the head learns: the representation it reads, which sets the signal a linear head can extract, and the comparison distribution it is trained on, which sets the direction of the reward. Every choice in the paper is one of the two, and the verified policy errors of Section 3.4 are the second variable’s final instance. A head of a few thousand parameters built this way beats GPT-4o by 6.6 points on VL-RewardBench at 32B, for about a thousandth of the compute of full backbone fine-tuning, and is level with GPT-4o on Multimodal RewardBench and MMRB2. At an equal pair count, the mined pairs teach a frozen head more than curated RLAIF-V pairs do. Figure 2: (a) The reward from a linear probe. A pair (image, prompt, real caption, same-image perturbation) passes once through the frozen backbone ϕ {\color[rgb]{0.0078,0.3125,0.4883}\phi} ; the layer- N − k {\color[rgb]{0.0078,0.3125,0.4883}N{-}k} states are mean-pooled over response tokens into h {\color[rgb]{0.0078,0.3125,0.4883}h} and scored by a bias-free head w {\color[rgb]{0.6523,0.4141,0}w} , trained with in-batch matrix Bradley–Terry; the sampler q neg {\color[rgb]{0.0039,0.418,0.3047}q_{\mathrm{neg}}} is the only place supervision enters. (b) One turn of the bootstrap loop ( Section 3.4 ): cheap verifiers label the policy’s own Best-of- N N candidates and the same head is retrained on the minted pairs. Blue frozen, orange trained, green supervision. Because the backbone is frozen, the objective is transparent enough to say what that number is. It is ranking noise-contrastive estimation over fixed features ( Gutmann and Hyvärinen, 2010 ; Ma and Collins, 2018 ) , so with a fixed quadratic penalty it is convex with a unique minimizer, characterized as an average of the negative sampler’s difference vectors weighted by how badly the head still misorders each pair ( Section 2.2 ). AdamW does not optimize that fixed objective, so where the trained heads land is measured rather than derived. In our runs no training-side change (pool size, steps, curriculum, loss form or optimizer setting) moves the benchmark by more than .014, so the representation and the sampler are the two choices that matter. The representation is the backbone’s, and our findings about it hold across backbones. On four Qwen3-VL sizes and on a second family, GLM-4.1V-9B, the best probe layer sits well below the top, twelve layers down for 8B, 32B and GLM-4.1V-9B. The same recipe with no re-tuning lifts each of them above its own untrained judge ( Section 3.2 ). The sampler is the other choice, and it is where the benchmark stops being informative. Which pairs train the head decides which reward it learns. Two probes trained on disjoint subsets of the same perturbations, split by whether CLIP can see the edit, reach similar benchmark accuracy and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging ( Fig. 1 b). Deployed for Best-of- N N reranking, benchmark rank orders utility in neither direction, and where the probe does beat majority vote, by 7 to 11 points, a training-free log-likelihood judge matches it. The analysis leaves one sampler to try: the policy’s own errors. We mint those labels with cheap verifiers on Best-of- N N candidates, for captions and for generated images; the resulting head cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points below the base Qwen3-VL-2B and 8B generators, while its VL-RewardBench accuracy falls below that of the probe it replaced ( Fig. 1 c). One DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) turn on the policy’s own pairs also cuts its hallucination by 3 to 6 CHAIR ( Rohrbach et al., 2018 ) points at no QA cost ( Table 8 ). Our contributions combine probing, negative sampling and self-improvement, each studied on the policy side before ( Section 4 ), into one reward-side recipe that uses no human preference label. (i) Probed, not trained in: a frozen vision-language backbone with a linear head (2,048 parameters at 2B) at a depth set by the backbone, at or above GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B ( Section 3.2 ). (ii) Supervision as a sampler: same-image perturbations written as a mixture of operators that apply to captions and to rendered images alike, with an argument for which reward direction they select and an ablation of the operators in both modalities ( Section 2.2 , Table 3 ). (iii) What the score tracks: benchmark accuracy plateaus under every training-side change we tried, the learned direction is set by the sampler, and benchmark rank predicts Best-of- N N rank in neither direction ( Sections 3.3 and 3.3 ). (iv) A bootstrap loop that replaces annotators with cheap verifiers on the policy’s own candidates, the one supervision that moved deployment, shown for captions and for image generation ( Section 3.4 ).

Editing one fact inside the same response holds author, length and style fixed by construction. These negatives cost nothing to label: the caption operators are string edits with no model in the loop, and the 22k-pair bank builds in 10 seconds on one CPU core. Rendering the image arm’s 1,212 pairs takes 5 GPU-hours ( Appendix K ).

sections.heading: Why perturbations provide useful supervision.
sections.text: Independent negatives from the caption marginal, our 𝒯 × \mathcal{T}_{\times} , make s ⋆ s^{\star} the image–caption pointwise mutual information up to a constant ( Section I.2 ): a score of topic association, which can rank an accurate and an inaccurate response on the same topic equally. A same-context edit changes one fact and nothing else. In the stylized model of Section I.3 the quality factor cancels from the PMI score, while the edited pairs recover the correct ordering with margin log ⁡ η 1 − η \log\frac{\eta}{1-\eta} even when a fraction 1 − η 1-\eta of the originals is wrong. Perturbations thus supply one quality comparison, an original above its degraded copy, without requesting a judgment. Corollary 1 (the sampler’s pair law sets the direction) . With the penalty λ 2 ​ w ⊤ ​ D ​ w \frac{\lambda}{2}w^{\top}Dw , the population minimizer of Eq. 2 satisfies D ​ w ⋆ = β λ ​ 𝔼 ​ [ σ ⁡ ( − β ​ w ⋆ ⁣ ⊤ ​ d ) ​ d ] , d = h + − h − , D\,w^{\star}\;=\;\frac{\beta}{\lambda}\;\mathbb{E}\big[\,\sigma(-\beta\,w^{\star\top}d)\;d\,\big],\qquad d=h^{+}-h^{-}, (5) the expectation over the pair law of the matrix loss: D ​ w ⋆ Dw^{\star} is the mean difference vector of the sampler’s pairs, each weighted by the probability the head still misorders it, so two samplers with the same perturbations but different pair laws give different heads in general. The law of the differences, not their span, sets the direction; this is how the two CLIP-split heads of Section 3.3 can reach similar benchmark accuracy while differing by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. Nothing in the objective sets the head’s length coefficient to zero, and Section 3.2 finds it with opposite signs at 2B and 8B under one sampler. Finally, Eq. 4 orders a policy’s own samples by a ratio against the perturbation process, so it ranks them by how unlike a perturbation each one looks and has no term for how wrong it is. The design hypothesis this leaves is that a sampler drawn from the policy’s own errors ranks them better: Section 3.3 measures how far the perturbation sampler falls short and Section 3.4 tests the hypothesis.

sections.heading: 2.3 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We build pairs from 70k PixMo web captions ( Deitke et al., 2024 ) and train heads on Qwen3-VL Instruct backbones at 2B, 4B, 8B and 32B, with the same negative bank and a frozen vision tower at every size. The headline recipe is the 2B backbone at probe layer N − 4 N{-}4 , head only, 200 steps of 256 pairs with AdamW at learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} and weight decay 0.01 0.01 ; every later run changes one element of it, and the curated comparison set is RLAIF-V ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Every head trains on the same schedule of 256 pairs per step, so two runs are compared at equal pairs seen along the training timeline ( Fig. 3 , right). We evaluate on Multimodal RewardBench ( Yasunaga et al., 2025 ) , VL-RewardBench ( Li et al., 2025 ) and MMRB2 ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , with GPT-4o ( OpenAI, 2024 ) as the anchor on all three and no re-tuning between them. Per-benchmark pair counts, the MMRB2 scoring construction and the confidence bands are in Appendix C . For Best-of- N N we sample N = 16 N{=}16 candidates from a Qwen3-VL-2B or 8B policy over 2,500 prompts of COCO captioning ( Lin et al., 2014 ) , MathVista ( Lu et al., 2024 ) , MMMU ( Yue et al., 2024 ) and Claude-written hard questions on COCO images. We measure CHAIRs ( Rohrbach et al., 2018 ) or exact match against six training-free controls, from random to the oracle, with 95% confidence intervals from a paired bootstrap over prompts.

sections.heading: 3.1 Two Choices Set the Accuracy: The Probe Layer and the Sampler
sections.text: Two choices set the accuracy, and neither is an optimizer setting: the probe layer alone adds 5.8 trainable points over the last layer, and mined negatives beat curated RLAIF-V pairs by 3.5 at equal pair count. Table 2 puts those two and every other ablation of the paper on one backbone under one recipe. Every number is a real end-to-end run except the layer sweep that nominated the probe depth: linear heads trained briefly on precomputed hidden states of every layer, a relative instrument that appears only in Fig. 3 and Appendix D . Figure 3: Left: layer-sweep trainable accuracy against layers below the top for 2B / 4B / 8B / 32B (bands: 75% binomial intervals); the optimum is never the last layer, and sweep numbers rank depths within a model only. Right: Multimodal RewardBench pair accuracy over the first 250 steps by negative type (2B full fine-tune, 674-pair eval subset): same-image perturbations transfer, cross-image negatives fall below the untrained base, curated pairs plateau lower.

sections.heading: Probe depth.
sections.text: The best probe layer is never the top of the network: it is N − 4 N{-}4 for 2B, N − 6 N{-}6 for 4B and N − 12 N{-}12 for both 8B and 32B. That depth is chosen on Multimodal RewardBench trainable accuracy, so we treat that benchmark as development throughout and VL-RewardBench and MMRB2, which no choice in the recipe has seen, as the transfer evidence. The gap over the last layer is 3 to 7 points in the layer sweep ( Fig. 3 ) and 5.8 trainable points on the real 4B run. The optimum deepens from 2B to 8B and then holds at twelve layers below the top for 8B, 32B and GLM-4.1V-9B (36, 64 and 40 layers), while the 36-layer 4B peaks at N − 6 N{-}6 , so the depth is set by the backbone and not by its layer count; each peak is a plateau several layers wide ( Appendix D ).

sections.heading: Negative construction.
sections.text: We find that same-image perturbations transfer in both modalities and that cross-image negatives do not ( Table 3 ). For text, 𝒯 × \mathcal{T}_{\times} alone reaches 99% training accuracy and falls below the untrained base on the benchmark, because it amplifies a length and style shortcut the same-image operators mostly remove: that head scores .224 on the length-sensitive safety/bias column against .451. For images the replica is exact, with the deranged negative transferring nothing to MMRB2 text-to-image (52.7 against a label prior of 53.2) while the same-seed planted edit accounts for all of it (56.0). Perturbation density and the operator mix are in Appendix D .

sections.heading: Every training-side change leaves the benchmark within .014 of the recipe.
sections.text: Changing the loss form or the negative composition, training on four times the pairs or for twice the steps, or ordering the negatives from easy to hard or from hard to easy moves a real 2B run by at most .014. In the sweep setting, changing the negative pool or the temperature schedule moves it by less than .005. The sharpest row is a 540-configuration grid over head learning rate, β \beta and weight decay: all 540 reach .995 or better in distribution, and selecting among them out of distribution changes the benchmark by .0003.

sections.heading: Mined negatives against curated pairs at a matched pair budget.
sections.text: At 15k pairs the mined-negative head is 3 to 4 trainable points ahead of curated RLAIF-V pairs on Multimodal RewardBench and 2 to 5 on VL-RewardBench, including the hallucination split RLAIF-V was built for ( Table 5 ). Unfreezing the backbone on the same 15k curated pairs recovers 11 points overall to .613: a frozen head matches full fine-tuning on mined-negative data where real pairs need the unfrozen model ( Appendix D ).

sections.heading: What the columns mean.
sections.text: The safety/bias column of Multimodal RewardBench is a length artifact, the one reward models are known to carry ( Singhal et al., 2024 ) . A head trained on same-image perturbations, two thirds of which match length exactly, scores .998 on it at 2B and .19 at 8B, where its correlation with response length flips sign. The gap is not seed noise: eight layer-sweep seeds give .967 ± .007 .967\pm.007 at 2B and .569 ± .013 .569\pm.013 at 8B, the same ordering ( Appendix C ). We therefore compare heads on the five trainable categories, where the 8B probe’s .659 overall against .708 at 2B becomes .658 against .602.

sections.heading: Same benchmark score, different reward.
sections.text: We train two probes on the two extreme quartiles of the same mined-negative data, ranked by the drop in CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) image–text cosine from the real to the perturbed caption, 15k pairs each at 2B. They reach similar accuracy on Multimodal RewardBench, .597 against .603 trainable, and then separate three ways ( Fig. 1 b): VL-RewardBench hallucination 72.0 against 78.4, reasoning 63.4 against 56.8, and as Best-of- N N scorers the CLIP-visible head beats probe-8B on CHAIRs by 3.8 points while losing 2.9 on QA. The same pattern, a small benchmark gap against a large hallucination gap, holds across sizes, consistent with Corollary 1 : the two samplers differ from the positives along different coordinates, and the benchmark does not separate them.

sections.heading: Whether a scorer helps Best-of- N N depends on the pool, not on its benchmark score.
sections.text: Across eight captioning and QA cells and a hard-QA ladder, a probe’s benchmark accuracy does not predict how much it improves Best-of- N N selection, in either direction ( Tables 6 and F ). On captioning every mined-negative probe stays at greedy level where the oracle reaches .06 to .09 CHAIRs, and on MathVista and MMMU, where candidate agreement tracks correctness, majority vote is 1.4 to 3.8 points ahead of the probe, whose one positive role there is as a vote weighter. Where the 8B generator is confidently wrong instead (majority wrong on 32% of prompts), every external scorer beats majority vote: probe-2B by 10.8 points, probe-8B by 7.2 and the training-free log-likelihood judge by 9.2, all with 95% CIs excluding zero. The trained head does not significantly beat the training-free judge: probe-2B against log-likelihood is + 1.6 +1.6 to + 2.1 +2.1 points with CIs including zero, and probe-2B beats probe-8B by 3.6 points, the reverse of their benchmark order. What decides the gain is the pool: whether the generator’s majority can be trusted, and so whether any external scorer should replace the vote. The benchmark measures neither.

sections.heading: 3.4 Learning from the Policy’s Own Errors: Better Deployment, Lower Benchmarks
sections.text: Figure 4: One turn of the loop. (a) CHAIRs@16 per captioning cell (hatched: verified probe trained without COCO-2). (b) Judging (VL-RewardBench) against ranking ( Δ \Delta CHAIRs vs greedy). Figure 2 b changes one element of the recipe of Section 2.1 , the negative sampler: the policy’s own Best-of- N N candidates, labelled by a cheap verifier, are paired correct against wrong for the same prompt. We train the head to separate verified successes from failures among the policy’s own outputs, the comparison that Best-of- N N selection makes at deployment. It lowers captioning CHAIRs where the perturbation probes did not: a head trained on 3,462 such pairs cuts CHAIRs by 5.1 points against greedy and by 4.1 points on a task it never trained on ( Fig. 1 c, Fig. 4 a, Table 7 ). On QA it matches probe-8B as a selector, so the utility claim rests on captioning, the open-ended task where no vote is available. CHAIR is both harvest label and metric, so the gain is in absent COCO-object mentions rather than faithfulness at large ( Appendix A ). The verified head is the weakest judge of the three heads ( Fig. 4 b) on VL-RewardBench, .615 against .669 and .682 for the perturbation probes, yet the one that ranks the policy’s captions below greedy’s hallucination rate (the other benchmarks in Table 7 ). Both follow from the sampler: 70% of the verified pairs are QA correctness pairs, so the categories they do not cover fall while math rises. The two rewards differ because the two comparisons do. Benchmark pairs contrast other models’ responses on annotator-chosen errors, close to what perturbations produce; verified pairs contrast this policy’s own successes and failures. In our runs the head trained on the second kind improves candidate selection and loses VL-RewardBench accuracy. Serving both the benchmark and the deployment is open: train on the union of the two samplers, give the head more than one direction, or draw benchmark pairs from the policy under deployment.

The label adds little over random pairs, so the selector’s effect on the actor is still to be shown ( Appendix G ). A head trained on 3,000 verifier-minted pairs is + 5.4 +5.4 at 8B (95% CI + 0.5 +0.5 to + 10.3 +10.3 ), 2.4 points above CLIP and 2.9 above the mined-negative image heads on the same prompts. The two verified heads cross over as MMRB2 judges, so here too the better ranker is the worse judge.

sections.heading: 4 Related Work
sections.text: Multimodal reward models and the benchmarks that rank them. A multimodal reward model is built by annotating preference pairs and fitting a scorer on them, from LLaVA-RLHF and RLHF-V ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2024 ) to MM-RLHF’s 120k human comparisons ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) and the scoring heads of IXC-2.5-Reward and UnifiedReward ( Zang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Removing the annotator usually means a model in their place ( Bai et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) ; we use a sampler, as hallucination-injection DPO does for the policy ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2023b ) . Multimodal RewardBench ( Yasunaga et al., 2025 ) , VL-RewardBench ( Li et al., 2025 ) and MMRB2 ( Hu et al., 2025 ) rank those models and generative judges ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Xiong et al., 2025 ) by pairwise accuracy against human labels ( Lambert et al., 2025 ; Malik et al., 2026 ; Frick et al., 2025 , cf.) . We take them as given and ask what the number measures. In text, policies optimized toward reward models of similar accuracy can perform quite differently ( Wen et al., 2025 ) , while an outcome reward model’s score tracks downstream accuracy better than validation loss does ( Qi et al., 2026 ) ; we ask when a reward model’s own benchmark score stops tracking deployment. Probing and probe depth. The scorer we set against those judges is a probe, and linear probes are classically an analysis tool for encoders ( Alain and Bengio, 2017 ; Tenney et al., 2019 ; Burns et al., 2023 ) ; intermediate layers often give better features than the last ( Skean et al., 2025 ) . LLaVA-Reward ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) is the closest prior use of a probe as a reward, mixing depths through a cross-attention module trained on annotated preferences; ours is a 2,048-parameter head with no label. Density-ratio estimation and negative sampling. A probe on a frozen backbone approximates a density ratio, which noise-contrastive estimation fits against a noise distribution ( Gutmann and Hyvärinen, 2010 ; van den Oord et al., 2018 ) that the negative-sampler literature designs to shape the representation ( He et al., 2020 ; Robinson et al., 2021 ; Kalantidis et al., 2020 ; Wang and Isola, 2020 ) , and in vision-language models as word-order and attribute swaps of the true caption ( Yuksekgonul et al., 2023 ; Hsieh et al., 2023 ) . With frozen features those choices act only through the objective. Closest to our objective is Fan et al. (2026) , a label-free in-batch Bradley–Terry reward on text with web continuations as the negative process; their invariance theorem gives a nuisance’s coefficient in the unrestricted optimum, which Proposition 1 restates for our matrix loss. Best-of- N N and learning from self-generated data. A reward built from that ratio is then used, like a verifier ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ; Uesato et al., 2022 ; Lightman et al., 2024 ) , under optimization pressure, and proxy rewards degrade under it ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Coste et al., 2024 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ) . We locate an earlier failure, before any pressure is applied, where the proxy’s benchmark score does not predict its Best-of- N N value ( Beirami et al., 2025 ) against self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . Expert iteration and STaR ( Anthony et al., 2017 ; Zelikman et al., 2022 ; Singh et al., 2024 ) improve a policy on its own verified outputs, and GKD ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) diagnoses the train–inference mismatch on the policy side; ours is the reward-side analogue.

sections.heading: 5 Concluding Remarks
sections.text: Frozen vision-language representations support strong reward modeling with only a linear head and caption perturbations, but probe depth and training comparisons determine which signals the head extracts. Similar benchmark scores can conceal different specializations, and higher preference accuracy need not yield better Best-of- N N selection. Retraining on verified policy outputs improves caption selection while lowering benchmark accuracy, so the supervision that helps deployment is drawn from the policy’s own errors. Anyone choosing a reward model should test how well it picks the best of their own policy’s samples, and a paper that reports one should state which pairs it was trained on.

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations and Broader Impacts
sections.text: Our approach lowers the additional training and preference-annotation requirements for multimodal reward modeling by learning a small scoring head over a frozen backbone. This may make task-specific reward models more accessible to researchers and practitioners with limited annotation budgets, while retaining the inference cost of the underlying backbone. Constructing training comparisons explicitly also makes the intended supervision easier to inspect and revise. The broader implication concerns how reward models are evaluated and selected. Our experiments show that higher preference-benchmark accuracy need not yield better selection of a policy’s outputs. Reporting the training comparison distribution alongside deployment-specific evaluations can therefore support more informed model selection. Conversely, using benchmark performance alone to justify deployment risks overlooking systematic errors and shortcuts, including response-length biases. These benefits have a limited demonstrated scope. Our experiments cover two backbone families, and verifier-based adaptation is evaluated for one round. Captioning improvements are measured with CHAIR, which also supplies the training labels; they establish fewer absent COCO-object mentions rather than general factuality or preserved informativeness, and a CHAIR-independent metric such as POPE ( Li et al., 2023 ) would be needed to settle the latter. Best-of- N N cells are single-seed, the hard-QA set was written and verified by one LLM family, and our Multimodal RewardBench overall omits the withheld toxicity split ( Section 3.2 ). The method does not establish safety or fairness capabilities, and broader deployment requires independent evaluation of output quality, coverage, and task-specific failure modes.

sections.heading: Appendix B Reproducibility
sections.text: The recipe is fully specified by Eqs. 1 , 2 and 3 and the hyper-parameters of Section 2.3 and Appendix D : a frozen Qwen3-VL checkpoint, a probe layer, mean pooling over response tokens, and one bias-free linear head trained with AdamW for 200 steps. Every input is public. Positives are PixMo-Cap captions ( Deitke et al., 2024 ) ; negatives are string edits of those captions with no model in the loop, so the 22k-pair bank rebuilds in 10 seconds on one CPU core from the operator definitions in Appendix D . The curated comparison set is public RLAIF-V ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , and all three evaluation benchmarks ( Yasunaga et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ) are used as released, with the pair counts and the scoring construction stated per benchmark in Section 2.3 . Contamination is checked by a 256-bit difference hash of every training image against every evaluation image, counting a pair as a near-duplicate at ≤ 10 \leq 10 differing bits, plus exact prompt matching. Against Multimodal RewardBench the perturbation set shares 5 near-duplicate images of 4,711 (0.1%) and no prompt; against VL-RewardBench, the 1,000 MMRB2 prompt images and the 1,000 COCO Best-of- N N images it shares none. The image arm renders 1,212 PixMo-derived prompts with Qwen-Image, so its training images are generated and its prompts are not those of MMRB2. The same audit exposes the curated baseline: RLAIF-V pairs overlap VL-RewardBench on 326 of 1,247 rows and Multimodal RewardBench on 18, which is why every RLAIF-V-trained row also reports the decontaminated subset. Source for pair construction, training, every selector in the Best-of- N N tables and the plotting scripts behind every figure will be released with the paper.

sections.heading: Appendix C Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: Multimodal RewardBench releases 4,711 of its 5,211 pairs, the toxicity split being withheld, in eight categories; our overall number is therefore comparable to published ones only through the recomputation of Table 1 . VL-RewardBench has 1,247 pairs (general 181, hallucination 749, reasoning 317), of which 326 overlap the RLAIF-V training set, so we also score anything trained on RLAIF-V on the 921 clean rows. On the 326 overlapping rows the RLAIF-V fine-tunes score .80 against .60 to .64 for models that never saw the data; on the clean rows their lead disappears. MMRB2 has 1,000 judge-labelled pairs per task (text-to-image, editing, interleaved generation, reasoning; 996 reasoning pairs are scoreable). We score it with the prompt in the user turn and the response, images included, in the assistant turn, the construction the heads were trained on. A scalar reward is order-invariant, so its accuracy equals MMRB2’s dual-order accuracy; exact ties count 0.5. We also report reasoning on the 350-pair text-only-output subset, the convention that benchmark’s paper uses for scalar reward models. On the four-task average under this construction the 32B probe scores 59.9 and the same backbone used as a generative judge 64.6; GPT-4o as a judge scores 59.7. Scoring prompt and response in one user turn instead costs the text heads 2 to 3 points on reasoning and 5 to 9 on its text-only subset. The GPT-4o margins in Table 1 are quoted as unpaired standard errors because the benchmark papers do not release per-item predictions, so a paired interval is not available. Shaded bands in every figure are 75% binomial intervals of the plotted accuracy over its evaluation set; seed-to-seed spread of the heads is narrower than the line width. sections.heading: Appendix I Reading the Two Statements
sections.text: The convexity fact of Section 2.2 predicts that, when gradient descent runs on a fixed-penalty objective, initialization, step size and step count cannot move the minimizer. It predicts nothing about AdamW, whose stationary points depend on its preconditioner, and nothing about the negative pool, the hardness schedule or the temperature, each of which changes the population objective rather than the path to its minimizer. The temperature is the least obvious of these: writing u = β ​ w u=\beta w turns the weight decay into λ 2 ​ β 2 ​ ∥ u ∥ 2 \frac{\lambda}{2\beta^{2}}\lVert u\rVert^{2} , so β \beta acts as an effective regularization strength that rescales w ⋆ w^{\star} and tilts its direction. That those interventions nonetheless leave the benchmark where it was ( Section 3.1 ) is an empirical finding, and Eq. 5 explains it. Each intervention re-weights the same difference vectors, and on the benchmark’s pairs the re-weighted heads order alike. The CLIP split of Section 3.3 is the same equation evaluated at a re-weighting large enough to separate on hallucination. The value at the minimizer is the best linear separation of positives from negatives in the layer N − k N{-}k feature space, which is consistent with depth moving the plateau while optimizer settings do not; convexity fixes the endpoint of the fixed-penalty problem and not the distance to it, which is where initialization re-enters ( Section 3.4 ). Proposition 1 is stated for the decoupled objective because that is the one with a closed-form optimum, and for mutually absolutely continuous P P and Q Q because that is what keeps the log ratio finite. Our sampler does not satisfy the hypothesis: a caption of another image has probability zero as a caption of this one, so on those pairs the unrestricted optimum runs to ± ∞ \pm\infty and separates the two laws with unbounded margin. The in-distribution accuracy of the recipe is the finite-sample face of that, with all 540 configurations of Section 3.1 at .995 or better, and it is why we analyze the linear head through the fixed-penalty problem of Corollary 1 rather than through Eq. 4 . The diagonal terms alone would leave a context-dependent offset free, making scores comparable within a prompt and not across prompts; the matrix form removes that freedom, and our same-image-only ablation ( Section 3.1 ) confirms that the offset does not change within-prompt accuracy. The matrix form also decides what the target does with length. Write a response as content c c and length l l . If the negatives match the positives’ length law conditionally on content, p ​ ( l ∣ c ) = q ¯ ​ ( l ∣ c ) p(l\mid c)=\bar{q}(l\mid c) , then d ​ P / d ​ Q \mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}Q depends on c c alone and length drops out of Eq. 4 (cf. Fan et al., 2026 ). A matched marginal is not enough: with two contents and two lengths, the joint tables P = ( .4 .1 .1 .4 ) , Q = ( .1 .4 .4 .1 ) P=\begin{pmatrix}.4&.1\\ .1&.4\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q=\begin{pmatrix}.1&.4\\ .4&.1\end{pmatrix} share the length marginal ( .5 , .5 ) (.5,.5) and still have ratios 4 4 and 1 / 4 1/4 that depend on length. Our substitution edits hold length fixed pairwise and splice and shuffle shorten the negative, so the bank meets neither condition exactly and nothing makes the target of Eq. 4 length-free. sections.text: Training a head is the cheapest step in the study. Once the frozen backbone’s hidden states are stored, a 540-configuration grid at 2B fits in about nine GPU-minutes, and a single head is 200 steps of a d → 1 d\to 1 linear map. The 32B confirm run used FSDP over eight GPUs at effective batch 1,024. Kakade Affiliation: Harvard University Hanlin Zhang Affiliation: October 8, 2026 Affiliation: Harvard University Abstract Vision-language reward models are trained on annotated preference pairs, which are expensive to collect and can disagree with each other, and are ranked by benchmark accuracy. We build one with no human preference label: a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone, trained to score a web caption above a perturbed version of the same caption; labeled data enters only to select the layer. The layer is the decisive choice, worth 5.8 points over the last layer, and one recipe transferred without re-tuning beats or at least matches GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B, 6.6 points ahead on VL-RewardBench, from a few thousand parameters at about a thousandth of fine-tuning compute. At an equal pair budget, perturbations teach a frozen head 3 to 5 points more than curated RLAIF-V pairs. Because the backbone is frozen the objective is convex and the perturbation sampler specifies the reward, which the benchmark does not identify: two heads trained on disjoint halves of the same perturbations tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. Retraining the head on the policy’s own verifier-labelled candidates cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points and lifts image-generation pass rate by 5.4, while scoring lower on every reward benchmark. Together, an intermediate-layer probe, free same-image perturbations and a verifier-driven bootstrap turn give a recipe for multimodal reward modeling that needs no annotator, costs a fraction of fine-tuning, and is specified by the comparisons it is trained on rather than by a benchmark rank. Figure 1: Reward modeling with no human preference label. (a) A linear probe on a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone, trained on caption perturbations, beats or at least matches GPT-4o at 32B. (b) Two probes trained on disjoint halves of the same data tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points on hallucination judging: the sampler, not the score, sets the reward. (c) Retraining the head on the policy’s own verifier-labelled candidates cuts caption hallucination 5.1 CHAIR points below the base generators ( Section 3.4 ). 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning from human feedback ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) has made the reward model the channel through which preferences enter post-training. For vision-language models the same design is now standard: a scalar scorer over an image, a prompt and a response, trained on annotated preference pairs and ranked on preference benchmarks ( Yasunaga et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ) . The design has two costs: multimodal preference pairs are expensive to annotate and the annotations disagree with each other ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Once the model is built, benchmark accuracy is how it is compared, selected and trusted. VL-RewardBench accuracy correlates with Best-of- N N accuracy on MMMU-Pro for generative judges (Pearson’s r > 0.9 r>0.9 ; Li et al., 2025 ); what sets that number for a scalar reward model, and when it stops predicting deployment, is the question this paper takes up. Text reward models show that a reward is a comparison before it is a number: Bradley–Terry training identifies a reward only up to a shift that may differ across prompts ( Bradley and Terry, 1952 ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , so a score of .8 has no stable meaning across prompts, candidate pools or checkpoints. The scalar hides the relative preference that was always the operative signal ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Zhang, 2026 ) , so what a reward model learns is set by which comparisons it is trained on. And those comparisons need no annotator: web continuations as chosen against in-batch continuations as rejected train a text reward model with no label at all ( Fan et al., 2026 ) . We take both findings to the vision-language setting, make the comparison the object of study, and remove the human labels entirely. The reward model is a linear head on the hidden states of an intermediate layer of a frozen backbone, trained by in-batch Bradley–Terry ( Bradley and Terry, 1952 ) against same-image perturbations of web captions or same-seed re-renders of a perturbed prompt ( Fig. 2 , Section 2 ). The claim is about the training data: the probe layer is selected on one labeled benchmark, which we therefore treat as development and never as transfer evidence, and the loop of Section 3.4 uses verifier labels, not annotators. Two things then decide what the head learns: the representation it reads, which sets the signal a linear head can extract, and the comparison distribution it is trained on, which sets the direction of the reward. Every choice in the paper is one of the two, and the verified policy errors of Section 3.4 are the second variable’s final instance. A head of a few thousand parameters built this way beats GPT-4o by 6.6 points on VL-RewardBench at 32B, for about a thousandth of the compute of full backbone fine-tuning, and is level with GPT-4o on Multimodal RewardBench and MMRB2. At an equal pair count, the mined pairs teach a frozen head more than curated RLAIF-V pairs do. Figure 2: (a) The reward from a linear probe. Blue frozen, orange trained, green supervision. Because the backbone is frozen, the objective is transparent enough to say what that number is. It is ranking noise-contrastive estimation over fixed features ( Gutmann and Hyvärinen, 2010 ; Ma and Collins, 2018 ) , so with a fixed quadratic penalty it is convex with a unique minimizer, characterized as an average of the negative sampler’s difference vectors weighted by how badly the head still misorders each pair ( Section 2.2 ). AdamW does not optimize that fixed objective, so where the trained heads land is measured rather than derived. In our runs no training-side change (pool size, steps, curriculum, loss form or optimizer setting) moves the benchmark by more than .014, so the representation and the sampler are the two choices that matter. The representation is the backbone’s, and our findings about it hold across backbones. On four Qwen3-VL sizes and on a second family, GLM-4.1V-9B, the best probe layer sits well below the top, twelve layers down for 8B, 32B and GLM-4.1V-9B. The same recipe with no re-tuning lifts each of them above its own untrained judge ( Section 3.2 ). The sampler is the other choice, and it is where the benchmark stops being informative. Which pairs train the head decides which reward it learns. Two probes trained on disjoint subsets of the same perturbations, split by whether CLIP can see the edit, reach similar benchmark accuracy and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging ( Fig. 1 b). Deployed for Best-of- N N reranking, benchmark rank orders utility in neither direction, and where the probe does beat majority vote, by 7 to 11 points, a training-free log-likelihood judge matches it. The analysis leaves one sampler to try: the policy’s own errors. We mint those labels with cheap verifiers on Best-of- N N candidates, for captions and for generated images; the resulting head cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points below the base Qwen3-VL-2B and 8B generators, while its VL-RewardBench accuracy falls below that of the probe it replaced ( Fig. 1 c). One DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) turn on the policy’s own pairs also cuts its hallucination by 3 to 6 CHAIR ( Rohrbach et al., 2018 ) points at no QA cost ( Table 8 ). Our contributions combine probing, negative sampling and self-improvement, each studied on the policy side before ( Section 4 ), into one reward-side recipe that uses no human preference label. (i) Probed, not trained in: a frozen vision-language backbone with a linear head (2,048 parameters at 2B) at a depth set by the backbone, at or above GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B ( Section 3.2 ). (ii) Supervision as a sampler: same-image perturbations written as a mixture of operators that apply to captions and to rendered images alike, with an argument for which reward direction they select and an ablation of the operators in both modalities ( Section 2.2 , Table 3 ). (iii) What the score tracks: benchmark accuracy plateaus under every training-side change we tried, the learned direction is set by the sampler, and benchmark rank predicts Best-of- N N rank in neither direction ( Sections 3.3 and 3.3 ). A multimodal reward model is built by annotating preference pairs and fitting a scorer on them, from LLaVA-RLHF and RLHF-V ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2024 ) to MM-RLHF’s 120k human comparisons ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) and the scoring heads of IXC-2.5-Reward and UnifiedReward ( Zang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Removing the annotator usually means a model in their place ( Bai et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) ; we use a sampler, as hallucination-injection DPO does for the policy ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2023b ) . Multimodal RewardBench ( Yasunaga et al., 2025 ) , VL-RewardBench ( Li et al., 2025 ) and MMRB2 ( Hu et al., 2025 ) rank those models and generative judges ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Xiong et al., 2025 ) by pairwise accuracy against human labels ( Lambert et al., 2025 ; Malik et al., 2026 ; Frick et al., 2025 , cf.) . We take them as given and ask what the number measures. In text, policies optimized toward reward models of similar accuracy can perform quite differently ( Wen et al., 2025 ) , while an outcome reward model’s score tracks downstream accuracy better than validation loss does ( Qi et al., 2026 ) ; we ask when a reward model’s own benchmark score stops tracking deployment. Probing and probe depth. The scorer we set against those judges is a probe, and linear probes are classically an analysis tool for encoders ( Alain and Bengio, 2017 ; Tenney et al., 2019 ; Burns et al., 2023 ) ; intermediate layers often give better features than the last ( Skean et al., 2025 ) . LLaVA-Reward ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) is the closest prior use of a probe as a reward, mixing depths through a cross-attention module trained on annotated preferences; ours is a 2,048-parameter head with no label. Density-ratio estimation and negative sampling. A probe on a frozen backbone approximates a density ratio, which noise-contrastive estimation fits against a noise distribution ( Gutmann and Hyvärinen, 2010 ; van den Oord et al., 2018 ) that the negative-sampler literature designs to shape the representation ( He et al., 2020 ; Robinson et al., 2021 ; Kalantidis et al., 2020 ; Wang and Isola, 2020 ) , and in vision-language models as word-order and attribute swaps of the true caption ( Yuksekgonul et al., 2023 ; Hsieh et al., 2023 ) . With frozen features those choices act only through the objective. Closest to our objective is Fan et al. (2026) , a label-free in-batch Bradley–Terry reward on text with web continuations as the negative process; their invariance theorem gives a nuisance’s coefficient in the unrestricted optimum, which Proposition 1 restates for our matrix loss. Best-of- N N and learning from self-generated data. A reward built from that ratio is then used, like a verifier ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ; Uesato et al., 2022 ; Lightman et al., 2024 ) , under optimization pressure, and proxy rewards degrade under it ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Coste et al., 2024 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ) . We locate an earlier failure, before any pressure is applied, where the proxy’s benchmark score does not predict its Best-of- N N value ( Beirami et al., 2025 ) against self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . Expert iteration and STaR ( Anthony et al., 2017 ; Zelikman et al., 2022 ; Singh et al., 2024 ) improve a policy on its own verified outputs, and GKD ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) diagnoses the train–inference mismatch on the policy side; ours is the reward-side analogue. 5 Concluding Remarks Frozen vision-language representations support strong reward modeling with only a linear head and caption perturbations, but probe depth and training comparisons determine which signals the head extracts. Similar benchmark scores can conceal different specializations, and higher preference accuracy need not yield better Best-of- N N selection. Retraining on verified policy outputs improves caption selection while lowering benchmark accuracy, so the supervision that helps deployment is drawn from the policy’s own errors. Anyone choosing a reward model should test how well it picks the best of their own policy’s samples, and a paper that reports one should state which pairs it was trained on.
